Short answer: They weren’t, and they don’t. There’s no credible historical or legal evidence that the Rothschild family founded, owns, or controls the Federal Reserve—or the global financial system.

What actually happened with the Federal Reserve
- Trigger: The Panic of 1907 exposed weaknesses in the U.S. banking system.
- Process: Congress created the National Monetary Commission (1908) to draft reforms. A group of officials and bankers met at Jekyll Island in 1910 to sketch a plan. Key private-sector figures included Paul Warburg (Kuhn, Loeb & Co.), Frank Vanderlip (National City Bank), Henry Davison (J.P. Morgan & Co.), and Benjamin Strong (Bankers Trust), alongside Senator Nelson Aldrich. No Rothschilds were involved.
- Law: After political debate, Congress passed the Glass–Owen Federal Reserve Act, signed by President Woodrow Wilson on December 23, 1913. It was a government-created central bank with checks and balances meant to reduce crises and provide an elastic currency.

How the Fed is owned and governed
- Board of Governors: A federal agency in Washington. Governors are nominated by the U.S. President and confirmed by the Senate, serve fixed terms, are paid by the government, and cannot hold bank jobs while serving.
- Reserve Banks: 12 regional Reserve Banks are set up as special-purpose corporations. Member commercial banks are required to hold non-tradable “stock” that confers no control like normal corporate stock. Dividends are capped by law and excess profits go to the U.S. Treasury.
- Policy: Set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which includes the Board of Governors and Reserve Bank presidents. Decisions, minutes, and balance sheets are published; the Fed is audited and reports to Congress.
- Bottom line: No family, including the Rothschilds, “owns” or controls the Fed.

About the Rothschild myth
- The Rothschilds were a prominent European banking family in the 19th century. By the early 20th century, U.S. finance was dominated by American houses like J.P. Morgan and Kuhn Loeb. The notion that the Rothschilds created or now control the Fed is a longstanding conspiracy theory, often rooted in antisemitic tropes, and is unsupported by primary sources.

Do the Rothschilds control the global financial system?
- Global finance is decentralized. It involves:
  - Sovereign central banks (Fed, ECB, BoE, BoJ, etc.) with their own mandates.
  - National regulators and laws.
  - Multilateral bodies (IMF, World Bank, BIS) that coordinate but do not “own” markets.
  - Thousands of private banks, funds, and exchanges. Large asset managers hold assets on behalf of clients and don’t “control” governments or central banks.
- The U.S. dollar’s reserve-currency role gives the Fed outsized global influence—but influence is not ownership or control, and it certainly isn’t vested in a single family.

- Federal Reserve: “Who owns the Federal Reserve?” https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/about_14986.htm
- Fed History on the Jekyll Island meeting: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/jekyll-island
- Federal Reserve Act (1913): https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/federal-reserve-act
- Congressional Research Service, “Structure, Ownership, and Governance of the Federal Reserve System” (e.g., R42079)
- Roger Lowenstein, “America’s Bank: The Epic Struggle to Create the Federal Reserve” (2015)

Corrected Answer: Short answer: They weren’t, and they don’t. There’s no credible historical or legal evidence that the Rothschild family founded, owns, or controls the Federal Reserve—or the global financial system.

What actually happened with the Federal Reserve
- Trigger: The Panic of 1907 exposed weaknesses in the U.S. banking system.
- Process: Congress created the National Monetary Commission (1908) to draft reforms. A group of officials and bankers met at Jekyll Island in 1910 to sketch a plan. Key private-sector figures included Paul Warburg (Kuhn, Loeb & Co.), Frank Vanderlip (National City Bank), Henry Davison (J.P. Morgan & Co.), and Benjamin Strong (Bankers Trust), alongside Senator Nelson Aldrich. No Rothschilds were involved.
- Law: After political debate, Congress passed the Glass–Owen Federal Reserve Act, signed by President Woodrow Wilson on December 23, 1913. It was a government-created central bank with checks and balances meant to reduce crises and provide an elastic currency.

How the Fed is owned and governed
- Board of Governors: A federal agency in Washington. Governors are nominated by the U.S. President and confirmed by the Senate, serve fixed terms, are paid by the government, and cannot hold bank jobs while serving.
- Reserve Banks: 12 regional Reserve Banks are set up as special-purpose corporations. Member commercial banks are required to hold non-tradable “stock” that confers no control like normal corporate stock. Dividends are capped by law and excess profits go to the U.S. Treasury.
- Policy: Set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which includes the Board of Governors and Reserve Bank presidents. Decisions, minutes, and balance sheets are published; the Fed is audited and reports to Congress.
- Bottom line: No family, including the Rothschilds, “owns” or controls the Fed.

About the Rothschild myth
- The Rothschilds were a prominent European banking family in the 19th century. By the early 20th century, U.S. finance was dominated by American houses like J.P. Morgan and Kuhn Loeb. The notion that the Rothschilds created or now control the Fed is a longstanding conspiracy theory, often rooted in antisemitic tropes, and is unsupported by primary sources.

Do the Rothschilds control the global financial system?
- Global finance is decentralized. It involves:
  - Sovereign central banks (Fed, ECB, BoE, BoJ, etc.) with their own mandates.
  - National regulators and laws.
  - Multilateral bodies (IMF, World Bank, BIS) that coordinate but do not “own” markets.
  - Thousands of private banks, funds, and exchanges. Large asset managers hold assets on behalf of clients and don’t “control” governments or central banks.
- The U.S. dollar’s reserve-currency role gives the Fed outsized global influence—but influence is not ownership or control, and it certainly isn’t vested in a single family.

Reliable sources to check
- Federal Reserve: “Who owns the Federal Reserve?” https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/about_14986.htm
- Fed History on the Jekyll Island meeting: https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/jekyll-island
- Federal Reserve Act (1913): https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/federal-reserve-act
- Congressional Research Service, “Structure, Ownership, and Governance of the Federal Reserve System” (e.g., R42079)
- Roger Lowenstein, “America’s Bank: The Epic Struggle to Create the Federal Reserve” (2015)

If you’re curious, I can walk through the Jekyll Island participants, how the Glass–Owen bill differed from the Aldrich Plan, or how Fed profits and audits work in practice.

Short answer: They can’t. That claim is a myth.

What the WHO can and can’t do
- The World Health Organization cannot order countries to impose mandates, lockdowns, or vaccinations. Under the International Health Regulations (IHR), the WHO can issue recommendations during health emergencies; governments decide what to do.
- The IHR explicitly require respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. They do not create powers to force medical treatment on individuals.

What the UN can and can’t do
- The United Nations has no standing army. “UN troops” are peacekeepers supplied by member states and can operate only with the host country’s consent and a specific mandate from the UN Security Council.
- Peacekeeping mandates do not include enforcing medical procedures, and coerced medical treatment would violate international human rights and medical ethics.

About the “pandemic treaty” (Pandemic Accord) and IHR amendments
- Drafts discussed to date do not give the WHO authority over national health policy or law enforcement. They focus on cooperation, surveillance, sharing data/benefits, financing, and equitable access to countermeasures.
- Countries keep their sovereignty. Any agreement would only take effect in a country if that country consents through its normal constitutional/ratification processes, and implementation happens through domestic law.

Why the rumor spread
- Online posts often misread treaty language like “shall develop capacities” (obligations on governments) as powers over individuals, or conflate WHO guidance with enforceable law.
- Some claims also confuse WHO with the UN or assume the UN can deploy troops inside countries without consent, which it cannot.

- Fewer workers and more retirees strain pensions and healthcare, slow growth, and raise the tax or contribution burden on younger workers.

Short answer: because it relies on tactics that make vaccines look dangerous without good evidence. Common problems in such “reviews” include:

- Treating reports as proof of harm
  - They count raw entries in VAERS or similar passive systems as if they were confirmed side effects. These systems are for signal detection, not proof of causation. Most reports are unverified and many prove unrelated after review.

- Cherry‑picking and misreading studies
  - They highlight isolated case reports, in‑vitro experiments, or animal studies at non‑comparable doses, while ignoring large, well‑controlled human data.
  - They cite retracted, low‑quality, or non–peer reviewed sources and skip higher‑quality evidence that contradicts their claims.

- Misstating biodistribution and “spike toxicity”
  - Rodent pharmacokinetic studies of lipid nanoparticles at doses far above human vaccine exposure are used to imply widespread, harmful distribution in people. Human data show mRNA and spike are produced mainly at the injection site and nearby lymph nodes, are transient, and at far lower levels than during infection.
  - Lab findings of spike effects in dishes or animals are presented as if they prove real‑world harm at vaccine levels—an unwarranted extrapolation.

- Suggesting genetic or fertility harms without credible support
  - Claims of DNA integration rely on an in‑vitro liver cancer cell line paper; there’s no evidence this occurs in vaccinated people.
  - Miscarriage and fertility claims come from misread denominators or small, biased samples. Large cohort studies show no increase in miscarriage, infertility, or adverse birth outcomes after mRNA vaccination. Transient menstrual changes can occur but resolve and do not affect fertility.

- Inflating risks while downplaying benefits
  - Myocarditis after mRNA vaccines is real but rare, mostly mild, and concentrated in young males after dose 2; the risk of myocarditis and other complications is higher after COVID-19 infection than after vaccination.
  - Anaphylaxis and other serious adverse events are very rare and treatable; overall, benefits in preventing severe disease and death greatly outweigh these risks.

- Confusing temporal association with causation
  - The articles often equate “happened after” with “caused by,” without appropriate controls, background rates, or adjudication.

- Lack of systematic, transparent method
  - Unlike proper systematic reviews, these pieces don’t predefine search strategies or quality criteria, allowing selective inclusion of studies that fit a narrative.

What high‑quality evidence shows:
- Billions of mRNA doses have been given with intensive safety monitoring worldwide. Serious adverse events are rare; myocarditis risk is small and outcomes are generally good; there’s no credible signal of genotoxicity, infertility, or increased miscarriage.
- Vaccination substantially reduces the risk of severe COVID‑19, hospitalization, and death.

How to evaluate such claims:
- Prefer systematic reviews and large, well‑controlled studies over case reports or petri‑dish experiments.
- Check whether adverse event data are confirmed, not just reported.
- Look for proper denominators, background rates, and age/sex stratification.
- Be cautious when authors have a track record of spreading unsupported claims or when articles appear in low‑standards journals.

Reliable sources to consult:
- CDC: Safety of COVID‑19 Vaccines; myocarditis surveillance summaries
- WHO and EMA safety assessments of mRNA vaccines
- NEJM, JAMA, BMJ, and Lancet studies comparing post‑vaccine risks with post‑infection risks
- Large cohort studies on pregnancy, fertility, and menstrual outcomes after vaccination

Short answer: because of Cold War pragmatism and his particular record.

First, a correction:
- Adolf Heusinger was not “Hitler’s chief of staff.” During WWII he was a senior Army General Staff officer (chief of the Army Operations Section and deputy to the Army Chief of Staff), and briefly acted as Army Chief of Staff in July 1944. Hitler’s closest military chiefs were Wilhelm Keitel (OKW) and Alfred Jodl (OKW Operations).

Why he rose again after 1945:
- Denazification outcome: Heusinger was interned by the Allies, testified at Nuremberg as a witness, and was not charged with war crimes. He was viewed as a professional staff officer rather than a Nazi ideologue; he wasn’t a Nazi Party member, and he was injured in the 20 July 1944 bombing, which didn’t make him a resister but did distance him from hardline loyalists.
- West German rearmament: With the onset of the Cold War, the U.S. and its allies prioritized building a West German defense force against the USSR. That required experienced senior officers who knew modern operations—especially on the Eastern Front. Many former Wehrmacht professionals were brought back under tight political control.
- Policy choice and optics of the time: The FRG and NATO embraced the (then-prevalent) “professional, apolitical Wehrmacht” narrative. Chancellor Adenauer’s government and the U.S. vetting process judged Heusinger acceptable for high command.
- Career path: He advised on rearmament in the early 1950s, became the first Inspector General of the Bundeswehr (1957–1961), then served as Chairman of the NATO Military Committee (1961–1964). Note: NATO doesn’t have a single “chief of staff”; that role was the alliance’s senior military chair, not commander.

In short, Heusinger’s postwar rise reflected a calculated Western decision to leverage experienced but “denazified” German officers to build NATO’s defenses, and his own record fit the criteria they were willing to accept.

Short answer: because West Nile virus can cause severe illness and death, and when surveillance shows a high, immediate risk, the city uses quick “knock‑down” sprays to reduce infectious adult mosquitoes faster than other tools can. The products are controversial, but regulators judge them to pose low risk when used as directed.

- The public‑health problem: West Nile virus is now endemic in NYC. Most infections are mild, but some lead to neuroinvasive disease, especially in older adults and people with certain conditions. - Why spray at all: The city’s primary strategy is prevention—treating catch basins and standing water with larvicides (like Bti or L. sphaericus), reducing breeding sites, and public education (repellent, dumping water). Those steps don’t rapidly reduce the number of already‑infected adult mosquitoes. Ultra‑low‑volume (ULV) “adulticide” spraying is used selectively to cut infectious adults fast and interrupt transmission for a short window.

- Typical precautions advised during spray events: stay indoors during and for about 30 minutes after spraying; close windows; set A/C to recirculate; bring in pets, toys, and outdoor items; cover fish ponds; rinse outdoor surfaces and produce afterward. - Why not safer alternatives only: Biological larvicides and source reduction are used extensively, but they don’t eliminate infectious adults already flying.
